newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Palm Oil/Laurics - Asian prices seen consolidating.
newsitem.headline: Palm Oil/Laurics - Asian prices seen consolidating.

text.p: Most Asian palm and laurics oil markets are seen consolidating this week, except for Indonesian palm oil prices which may hold steady on tight supply, regional traders said on Monday.
Indonesian palm traders said the upside could be capped by possible oil imports from Malaysia.
They attributed the supply squeeze to players meeting their export commitments made when overseas' prices were higher than local values, and lower-than-expected production in some areas.
"Supply seems to be tight with some players not selling on the spot market because they don't have the oil," one trader in Indonesia said.
"Prices will be steady but there'll be no jumps."

Traders in Indonesia said the state logistics agency BULOG could import olein from Malaysia if domestic prices edged closer to 1,500 rupiah a kg. BULOG preferred local prices to be nearer to 1,400-1,450 rupiah for consumers, they said.
"If prices near 1,500 rupiah, I think BULOG will begin to bring in oil," one trader based in Indonesia added.
Indonesian palm olein finished last week at 1,460-65 rupiah a kg in Jakarta against 1,450 previously.
Palm oil prices in Singapore and Malaysia will probably range-trade this week while waiting for fresh fundamental data.
"We are expecting SGS and Caleb to announce supportive September export data this week to provide the market with a path," a dealer in Malaysia said.
Cargo surveyors SGS (M) Sdn Bhd will release the export data on Monday and Caleb Brett on October 1.
Talk of rising Malaysian palm oil production and a build-up of local stocks could see prices slide further in coming months.
A lack of strong export business could also undermine sentiment in palm oil, traders added.
Buying by India, the biggest customer for palm oil recently, may begin to tail off as its soybean harvest gets underway next month, Singapore traders said.

"You still go back to the same old questions. When will the Chinese buy? People are saying they should be buying soon after not buying much over the last few weeks. But they've been saying that for the past nine months," a Singapore commodity house trader said.
But stocks are beginning to build as demand slackens and it looks like Malaysian production will surge strongly in 1997.
"The key for the market is producer sentiment," a trader in Singapore said, adding plantation farms will have to decide to carry stocks until early next year or unload stocks now.
"If they sell it off, that will cause prices to sag," another dealer in Singapore added.
Malaysia's third month December futures contract which closed on Friday at 1,165 ringgit a tonne, may trade in a range between around 1,130 to 1,190 ringgit, dealer said.
Philippine coconut oil prices are expected to move in a narrow range as reports of low copra turnover prevail among local oil millers.

"There were reports of low copra turnover receipts which prompted some consumers to cover their requirements. We cannot quantify things but the news caused some buying among hand-to-mouth consumers who had postponed their purchases thinking supply would increase," said a Filipino trader.
Persistent rains in Mindanao in the southern Philippines where coconut plantations abound and delayed harvest may have caused the tightness in copra supply
The United Coconut Association of the Philippines said coconut oil was last traded at an average rate of $750 a tonne CIF for August/September and $727.50 for September/October.
(with contributions from Singapore/Jakarta/Manila)
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom 603-230-8911)
